notes.meaning: Solomon finished the temple, his royal palace, and everything else he had planned to build. Once the work was done, the Lord visited him a second time in a dream or vision, just as He had done years earlier at Gibeon. God came to give Solomon an answer to his prayer and to guide him for the next season of his reign.

The Lord told Solomon that He had heard his prayer at the temple's dedication. Solomon had built the physical building, but only God could make it holy by placing His name and presence there. God promised that His watchful care and His affection would rest upon the temple continually.

God set clear terms for Solomon and his future royal line. If Solomon stayed loyal to the Lord from the heart, like his father David, God would establish his royal family on the throne of Israel forever. David was not sinless, but his heart remained fully committed to the true God without turning to idols.

differ.view: The covenant with David is ultimately unconditional because God guaranteed its final fulfillment through Jesus Christ, but individual kings only enjoyed the kingdom's blessings if they remained obedient.
The promise to David's royal line is completely unconditional, meaning David's family never lost the divine right to the throne even when disobedience removed individual rulers like Solomon's sons.

notes.meaning: The Lord warned that if Solomon or his descendants completely turned their backs on Him to worship other gods, disaster would follow. God would uproot Israel from the promised land and abandon the very temple He had made holy. The nation would become an object of public mocking and shame among all other peoples.

Even though the temple was grand and admired by all, it would be left in ruins if the people abandoned God. Travelers passing by would gasp in shock and mock, wondering how such a holy place could be destroyed. The answer would be plain to all: the people brought ruin on themselves by forsaking the Lord who had rescued them from slavery in Egypt.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest changing the Hebrew word for 'high' to mean 'ruins,' but commentators note that ancient versions and manuscripts do not support this change.

notes.meaning: Solomon spent twenty years building the temple and his own palace. Hiram, the king of Tyre, had supplied Solomon with all the cedar, cypress, and gold he needed for these massive works. In return, Solomon gave Hiram twenty towns located in the northern region of Galilee.

Hiram traveled from Tyre to inspect the towns Solomon had given him, but he was disappointed with what he saw. He called the area the land of Cabul, an expression meaning displeasing or worthless. Hiram was a seafaring trader used to prosperous coastal cities, so inland farming towns held little value for him.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest the name Cabul originally referred to land held as a pledge or pawn for a loan, rather than being an insult about the quality of the soil.

notes.meaning: Hiram had sent Solomon one hundred and twenty talents of gold to help fund his grand building projects. This was an enormous amount of wealth that Solomon had to account for in their trade agreement. Giving the twenty towns was part of the royal settlement between the two kings.

Solomon organized a system of forced labor to carry out his extensive construction plans. He used these workers to build the temple, his palace, the terrace fortress known as the Millo, and the defensive wall of Jerusalem. He also used this labor force to fortify key military outposts across the land, including Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer.

Gezer had remained an independent Canaanite city until the king of Egypt attacked, captured, and burned it. Pharaoh wiped out its inhabitants and gave the ruined city as a wedding gift to his daughter when she married Solomon. Solomon then had the opportunity to rebuild it as a Hebrew fortress.

Solomon rebuilt and fortified Gezer along with Lower Beth-horon, Baalath, and Tamar in the desert. He also constructed storage cities to hold supplies, as well as bases for his war chariots and cavalry horses. He carried out every building project he wanted in Jerusalem, in the forests of Lebanon, and throughout his territory.

Non-Israelite peoples who still lived in the land—Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites—had survived earlier conquests. Solomon drafted their descendants into permanent forced labor for his building projects. This fulfilled ancient laws permitting foreign captives to serve as perpetual laborers.

Solomon did not force the Israelites into slave labor, because they were God's free covenant people. Instead, Israelites served as soldiers, government officials, chariot commanders, and cavalry leaders. A group of 550 Israelites served as the chief supervisors overseeing the entire workforce.

Solomon moved his wife, Pharaoh's daughter, out of the older City of David into the custom palace he had built for her. Only after completing her residence did he build the Millo, a major supporting terrace and defensive work in Jerusalem. This resolved the temporary housing arrangements from the beginning of his reign.

Solomon faithfully sponsored sacrifices three times a year at the temple altar during the major pilgrim festivals: Passover, Pentecost, and the Feast of Tabernacles. He also provided the incense to be burned before the Lord, with the priests carrying out the holy rituals on his behalf. With regular worship now taking place as God commanded, the work of the temple was truly complete.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars argue that early kings like Solomon functioned directly as priests by offering sacrifices and burning incense themselves, before such duties were restricted only to the Levites.

notes.meaning: Solomon established a seaport and built a fleet of trading ships at Ezion-geber on the Red Sea coast in Edom. Because Israel had little seafaring experience, King Hiram of Tyre sent skilled Phoenician sailors to man the ships alongside Solomon's men. This partnership allowed both nations to trade with distant lands.

The joint fleet sailed to the distant land of Ophir and brought back 420 talents of gold for King Solomon. This commercial voyage brought immense wealth into Jerusalem, confirming the prosperity of Solomon's kingdom. God used this trade to supply the resources Solomon needed to sustain his realm.
